title: Twelve stones (Joshua 3–4)
hook: the priests step into the Jordan first, and twelve stones are set up so children will ask "What mean ye by these stones?"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rahab, the woman on the wall. Your line was the scarlet cord. Did you do your one small thing for someone exposed? Today, the people cross the river. Day seven hundred.

The river is in flood. The book stops to tell us that: at harvest time the Jordan runs over all its banks. On the near side stands a whole people, with children, animals, everything they own. The instruction is strange. Nobody builds a bridge. Nobody waits for the water to drop. The priests carrying the ark of the covenant walk to the edge first, and step in. The moment their feet touch the water, the river upstream stops and stands up in a heap, and the people cross on dry ground. And then, before anyone moves on, Joshua asks for stones.
screen: `THE JORDAN IN FLOOD.` → `THE PRIESTS STEP IN FIRST.` → `THE RIVER STOPS.`

segments.voice: Twelve men are chosen, one from each tribe. Each goes back into the riverbed, to the spot where the priests are standing, picks up a stone, and carries it out on his shoulder. Joshua sets the twelve up at Gilgal, where they camp that night. Why? The text answers, and the answer is a question. These stones are a sign, so that when your children ask in time to come, "What mean ye by these stones?" you can tell them: the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark. The memorial is built to be asked about. A pile of river stones doesn't explain itself. Someone has to say, I'll tell you. If that sounds familiar, it should. The Torah does the same thing at Passover: when your children say to you, "What mean ye by this service?" From Egypt to the Jordan, remembering runs through a child's question and a parent's story. The Hebrew behind in time to come is machar, the everyday word for tomorrow. When your children ask you tomorrow. The book expects the question soon, from the next generation. And there's a second pile. Joshua also sets up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan, right where the priests' feet stood, and the text says they're there to this day. One pile on the bank for everyone to see and ask about. One in the river, where the priests stood and the crossing happened.
screen: `ONE STONE FOR EACH TRIBE.` · `BUILT TO BE ASKED ABOUT.` · `MACHAR: TOMORROW.` · then, large: `WHAT MEAN YE BY THESE STONES?` · then: `A SECOND PILE, UNDER THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep a small stone to remember something. If there's a stone nearby, a pebble from a plant pot, anything small and solid, pick it up. If not, choose any small object within reach. Hold it in your palm and feel its weight. Now choose what it's for: one crossing in your life, a time something gave way when you didn't expect it to. Don't tell the whole story to yourself. Just name it, and let the stone hold it. Sit with it in your hand. The bell holds the time.
Twelve stones. Carried out of the Jordan, one for each tribe, and set up so that children would ask what they mean. Today's word.
Your line: what mean these stones. Today, put your stone where someone might ask about it, and if they do, tell them the story. Day seven hundred.

howItsDone: At the Passover seder the story is told in answer to children's questions, and some families keep objects at home that prompt a story to be retold.

the water stops the moment your feet touch it.

fork.reveal: the river stops when the priests' feet touch the edge. they had to step into the flood before anything changed.

original.note: Hebrew: what are these stones? the children's question in Joshua 4:6.

trapdoor: what you thought: a monument to a miracle.
what it means: twelve stones, one per tribe, set up so that children would ask, and a parent would tell how the river stopped.
what a scholar hears: machar. when your children ask tomorrow: the same word Exodus 13:14 uses for a child's question about leaving Egypt.

notes: Verify JPS 1917 wording of Joshua 4:6 and Exodus 12:26 quotations.

Machar in Joshua 4:6 (and Exodus 13:14) is the ordinary word for 'tomorrow', rendered 'in time to come'; the trapdoor ties it to the Passover question. Exodus 12:26 itself does not use machar; the trapdoor says 'the same word the Torah uses for the child's question at Passover', which relies on Exodus 13:14. Confirm or reword.
The second pile in the riverbed follows Joshua 4:9; some commentators read the verses differently. Confirm the plain-sense telling.
'Twelve' and 'one from each tribe' are stated in Joshua 4:2–5.

Editor: trapdoor fixed (Exodus 12:26 has no machar; the word is in Exodus 13:14); cut 'here's a detail worth keeping', 'not far off in a museum' and 'seen by no one' (not in the text); generalization about 'the Jewish way of remembering' and 'Jews often' softened.
